subject: maths
title: Data and Graphs: Pictographs, Column Graphs and Dot Plots
seo_title: Year 4 Data and Graphs Worksheets: Pictographs, Column Graphs and Dot Plots (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Acquire data for categorical and discrete numerical variables to address a question of interest or purpose, using digital tools; represent data using many-to-one pictographs, column graphs and other displays or visualisations; interpret and discuss the information that has been created
meta_desc: Free Year 4 maths worksheets on data and graphs for the Australian Curriculum: tally marks and frequency tables, many-to-one pictographs (1 symbol = 2, 5 or 10), column graphs with scales of 2, 5 and 10, dot plots and survey conclusions. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Read the key or the scale first. One symbol or one gridline is often worth more than 1.
key_sub: If one symbol = 10, half a symbol = 5. A column halfway between 30 and 40 shows 35. A conclusion must match the data and the people you asked.
body_html:
Ask a question, then collect data

Start with a question, such as “How do Year 4 students travel to school?”. Then ask the right people and record every answer. Some data is in categories (words, such as bus or netball). Some data is numerical (numbers, such as how many books you read).

Record the answers with tally marks or in a spreadsheet, and write the totals in a frequency table. Then show the data in a pictograph, a column graph or a dot plot.

Tally marks and frequency tables

Draw one mark for each answer. The fifth mark goes across the other four. Count the groups in 5s, then add the single marks. The frequency is how many.

Many-to-one pictographs

In Year 4, one symbol stands for many: 2, 5 or 10. Read the key first. Count the symbols in 2s, 5s or 10s. Half a symbol is half of the key: if one symbol = 10, half = 5.

Example

How many more students chose netball than soccer?

Netball: 4 circles and a half = 45. Soccer: 3 circles = 30. 45 − 30 = 15.

Answer: 15 students

Column graphs

Find what the scale goes up in: 2s, 5s or 10s. Go across from the top of the column to the scale. If a column ends halfway between two gridlines, the number is halfway between them.

The pictograph and the column graph show the same data. To check two displays, read every category in both.

Dot plots

A dot plot shows numerical data. Each answer is one dot above a number line. The tallest stack is the most common answer.

Make conclusions the data supports

A conclusion must match the numbers and the people you asked.

ConclusionSupported?
Netball got the most votes in Year 4.Yes: it has the tallest column.
Netball got 15 more votes than soccer.Yes: 45 − 30 = 15.
Every Australian child likes netball best.No: only Year 4 was asked.
Nobody likes cricket.No: 20 students chose it.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading each symbol as 1Use the key: 4 circles of 10 = 40
Saying half a symbol = 1Half a symbol is half of the key
Counting grid spaces instead of reading the scaleRead the number on the scale
Reading a column between gridlines as the lower lineHalfway between 30 and 40 is 35
Counting the stacks on a dot plotCount every dot: one dot is one answer
Making a conclusion about people who were not askedOnly talk about the data you collected

faq.q: What do Year 4 students learn about data in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: They collect categorical and numerical data, record it in tables or spreadsheets, and show it in many-to-one pictographs, column graphs and dot plots. They then interpret the displays and discuss what the data shows.
It is a pictograph where one symbol stands for more than one, such as 2, 5 or 10. You use the key to work out each row, so 3 symbols with a key of 10 means 30.

faq.q: How do you choose a scale for a column graph?
faq.a: Look at the biggest number and choose a scale (such as 2s, 5s or 10s) that fits it in about 10 gridlines. If the numbers are all multiples of the scale, every column ends exactly on a line.

faq.q: What is the difference between categorical and numerical data?
faq.a: Categorical data is words or groups, such as favourite sport or how you travel to school. Numerical data is numbers, such as how many books you read or how many pets you have.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 3 groups of 5 and 3 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 3 = 18.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 5 groups of 5 and 2 more: 5 × 5 = 25, and 25 + 2 = 27.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 6 groups of 5 and 4 more: 6 × 5 = 30, and 30 + 4 = 34.
Each group of 5 is four lines with one line across. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks: 8 groups of 5 and 1 more: 8 × 5 = 40, and 40 + 1 = 41.
23 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 3, so look for 4 groups of 5 and 3 single marks. That is C. A shows 28 (one group of 5 too many); B shows 22 (one single mark is missing); D shows 24 (one single mark too many).

items.q: What number should go in the Frequency column for Mango?
items.e: The frequency is the number the tally marks show. Mango has 3 groups of 5 and 1 more: 3 × 5 = 15, and 15 + 1 = 16.

items.q: Which fruit got the fewest votes?
items.e: Orange has the shortest tally: 1 group of 5 and 1 more, so 6 votes. Apple has 8, the next fewest.

items.q: How many more votes did Mango get than Watermelon?
items.e: Mango 16 (3 groups of 5 and 1 more). Watermelon 11. How many more means subtract: 16 − 11 = 5. (Counting each tally group as 4 makes Mango 13, and 13 − 11 = 2.)

items.q: Every student in 4B voted once. How many students are in 4B?
items.e: Find the Mango frequency first: 16. Then add all the rows: 8 + 13 + 16 + 6 + 11 = 54.

items.q: How many students have 2 pets?
items.e: Find the row for 2 pets. The frequency is 7, so 7 students have 2 pets. The 2 is the number of pets, not the number of students.

items.q: What is the most common number of pets?
items.e: The biggest frequency is 9, in the row for 1 pet. So 1 pet is the most common answer. 9 is how many students, not how many pets.

items.q: How many students answered the survey?
items.e: Add the frequencies: 5 + 9 + 7 + 3 + 2 = 26 students. (10 adds the numbers of pets, 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. 21 leaves out the students with no pets.)

items.q: How many students have more than 2 pets?
items.e: More than 2 means 3 or 4 pets: 3 + 2 = 5 students. Do not include the students with exactly 2 pets (that gives 12).

items.q: How many cans did 4B collect?
items.e: Add the classes you know: 34 + 27 + 41 = 102. The total is 140, so 4B collected 140 − 102 = 38. (242 adds instead of subtracting. 42 comes from taking 0 from 2 in the ones.)

items.q: Which class collected 7 more cans than 4C?
items.e: 4C collected 27. 7 more is 27 + 7 = 34. 4A collected 34.

items.q: How many more cans did 4D collect than 4C?
items.e: 4D 41, 4C 27. How many more means subtract: 41 − 27 = 14. (26 comes from taking 1 from 7 in the ones instead of regrouping. 68 is the sum.)

items.q: Which survey question gives numerical data (answers that are numbers)?
c: How do you get to school?
How many books did you read last week?
items.e: “How many books did you read last week?” has number answers, such as 0, 2 or 5. The other questions have answers that are categories (words), such as netball, bus or Wattle.

items.q: Which survey question gives categorical data (answers that are words, not numbers)?
c: How many minutes do you read each night?
How many pets do you have?
How many people live in your house?
items.e: Favourite season gives answers like summer or winter. These are categories. The other questions ask “how many”, so the answers are numbers.

items.q: Cooper makes a tally of the cars that pass the school gate. He draws 6 groups of five and 4 single marks. How many cars has he counted?
items.e: 6 groups of five: 6 × 5 = 30. Then 4 more: 30 + 4 = 34 cars. (Counting each group as 4 gives 24 + 4 = 28.)

items.q: Ruby counted 23 votes for netball. How should she draw the tally?
items.e: 23 = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 3. Draw 4 groups of five (four lines and one across) and 3 single marks. Never leave 5 or more single marks: make another group of five. (2 groups and 3 marks is only 13.)

items.q: How many votes did Watermelon get?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 2 votes. The Watermelon row has 8 circles: 8 × 2 = 16 votes.
Look at the key: each star stands for 2 books. The Charlotte row has 3 stars and half a star: 3 × 2 = 6, and half of 2 is 1, so 6 + 1 = 7 books.

items.q: In this pictograph, what does half a square stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole square = 2 shells. Half a square is half of 2, which is 1 shell. (Half a symbol is not always 1: it is half of the key.)

items.q: Which row shows the most birds?
items.e: Every circle stands for the same number, so the row with the most circles shows the most. The Kookaburra row has 9 circles: 9 × 2 = 18 birds.
Look at the key: each star stands for 2 votes. Wombat: 8 × 2 = 16 and Platypus: 2 × 2 = 4. How many more means find the difference: 16 − 4 = 12 votes.

items.q: Which row shows 3 students?
items.e: Half a square is 1, so 3 students is 1 and a half squares. The Swimming row has 1 square and half a square: 1 × 2 = 2, and half of 2 is 1, so 2 + 1 = 3 students.

items.q: How many students ride a scooter to school?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 5 students. The Scooter row has 2 circles: 2 × 5 = 10 students.

items.q: Each star stands for 5 votes. Netball got 40 votes. How many stars should be in the Netball row?
items.e: Count in 5s until you reach 40: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40. That is 8 steps, so draw 8 stars. Check: 8 × 5 = 40. (Drawing 40 stars would mean each star stands for 1.)

items.q: How many cans did class 4C collect?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 5 cans. The 4C row has 1 square: 1 × 5 = 5 cans.

items.q: Which row shows the fewest ice blocks?
items.e: Every circle stands for the same number, so the row with the fewest circles shows the fewest. The Tue row has 1 circle: 1 × 5 = 5 ice blocks.
Look at the key: each star stands for 5 students. Swimming: 4 × 5 = 20 and Cricket: 2 × 5 = 10. How many more means find the difference: 20 − 10 = 10 students.

items.q: How many votes were there altogether?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 5 votes. Read every row: Mango 40, Watermelon 10, Orange 30, Apple 20, Banana 35. Add them: 40 + 10 + 30 + 20 + 35 = 135 votes.

items.q: How many points did Jacaranda House get?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 10 points. The Jacaranda row has 7 circles: 7 × 10 = 70 points.
Look at the key: each star stands for 10 tickets. The 4C row has 4 stars and half a star: 4 × 10 = 40, and half of 10 is 5, so 40 + 5 = 45 tickets.

items.q: In this pictograph, what does half a square stand for?
items.e: The key says one whole square = 10 points. Half a square is half of 10, which is 5 points. (Half a symbol is not always 1: it is half of the key.)

items.q: Each circle stands for 10 students. 45 students ride a bike to school. What should the Bike row show?
items.e: 45 = 40 + 5. 40 is 4 circles (4 × 10 = 40). 5 is half of 10, so add half a circle. Draw 4 and a half circles. (Drawing 45 circles would mean each circle stands for 1.)
Half a star is 5, so 35 tickets is 3 and a half stars. The 4C row has 3 stars and half a star: 3 × 10 = 30, and half of 10 is 5, so 30 + 5 = 35 tickets.

items.q: How many ice blocks were sold on Wednesday?
items.e: Look at the key: each square stands for 10 ice blocks. The Wed row has 2 squares and half a square: 2 × 10 = 20, and half of 10 is 5, so 20 + 5 = 25 ice blocks.

items.q: How many more students walk to school than ride a bike?
items.e: Look at the key: each circle stands for 10 students. Walk: 6 × 10 = 60 and Bike: 3 × 10 + 5 = 35. How many more means find the difference: 60 − 35 = 25 students.
Look at the key: each star stands for 10 cans. Read every row: 4A 30, 4B 70, 4C 45, 4D 55. Add them: 30 + 70 + 45 + 55 = 200 cans.

sets.title: Column graphs with scales of 2, 5 and 10

items.q: What does the scale on this column graph go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 2, 4, 6 … Each line is 2 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 2s. Each gridline is worth 2, not 1.

items.q: How many books did Mia read?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The column for Mia ends on the line for 18. So the answer is 18 books.

items.q: How many votes did the echidna get?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. The column for Echidna ends halfway between 2 and 4, so it shows 3. So the answer is 3 votes.

items.q: Which column shows 3 shells?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. Find 3 on the scale. The column for Leo ends halfway between 2 and 4, so it shows 3.

items.q: Which column shows the most students?
items.e: The column for Cricket is the tallest one. The column for Cricket ends on the line for 16.

items.q: How many more votes did the kangaroo get than the wombat?
items.e: The scale goes up in 2s. Kangaroo: 17. Wombat: 9. How many more means find the difference: 17 − 9 = 8 votes.

items.q: What does the scale on this column graph go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 5, 10, 15 … Each line is 5 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 5s. Each gridline is worth 5, not 1.

items.q: How many students ride a scooter to school?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. The column for Scooter ends on the line for 10. So the answer is 10 students.

items.q: How many cans did class 4B collect?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. The column for 4B ends on the line for 15. So the answer is 15 cans.

items.q: Which column shows the fewest votes?
items.e: The column for Mango is the shortest one. The column for Mango ends on the line for 5.

items.q: How many more shells did Kai find than Ruby?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. Kai: 30. Ruby: 5. How many more means find the difference: 30 − 5 = 25 shells.

items.q: How many students chose soccer or AFL?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. Soccer: 25. AFL: 10. Altogether means add: 25 + 10 = 35 students.

items.q: What does the scale on this column graph go up in?
items.e: Read the numbers on the scale: 0, 10, 20, 30 … Each line is 10 more than the one before, so the scale goes up in 10s. Each gridline is worth 10, not 1.

items.q: How many tickets did class 4A sell?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. The column for 4A ends halfway between 10 and 20, so it shows 15. So the answer is 15 tickets.

items.q: How many students ride a scooter to school?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. The column for Scooter ends halfway between 50 and 60, so it shows 55. So the answer is 55 students.

items.q: How many ice blocks were sold on Thursday?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. The column for Thu ends halfway between 10 and 20, so it shows 15. So the answer is 15 ice blocks.

items.q: Which column shows 35 votes?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. Find 35 on the scale. The column for Koala ends halfway between 30 and 40, so it shows 35.

items.q: How many more cans did class 4A collect than 4B?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. 4A: 75. 4B: 40. How many more means find the difference: 75 − 40 = 35 cans.

items.q: How many tickets did classes 4D and 4A sell altogether?
items.e: The scale goes up in 10s. 4D: 55. 4A: 10. Altogether means add: 55 + 10 = 65 tickets.

items.q: Which column shows the most points?
items.e: The column for Wattle is the tallest one. The column for Wattle ends on the line for 80.

sets.title: Compare displays and read dot plots

items.q: Mia will draw a pictograph of these votes: 40, 25, 35 and 50. She wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as she can. Which key should she use?
items.e: Every number is in the 5 times table, so a key of 5 gives whole symbols: 8, 5, 7 and 10. A key of 10 or 2 would need half symbols for 25 and 35. A key of 1 needs 150 symbols.

items.q: Jack will draw a pictograph of 60, 90, 40 and 70 students. He wants whole symbols only, and as few symbols as he can. Which key should he use?
items.e: Every number is a multiple of 10, so a key of 10 gives whole symbols: 6, 9, 4 and 7 (26 symbols). A key of 5 also works, but it needs twice as many symbols (52).

items.q: Kai will draw a column graph of 12, 18, 6 and 14 votes. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and he wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 1s needs 18 gridlines, which is too many. Counting in 2s needs 9 gridlines (2 to 18), and every number is even, so every column ends on a line. In 5s or 10s, 12, 18, 6 and 14 would end between lines.

items.q: Isla will draw a column graph of 35, 50, 20 and 45 tickets. Every column must end exactly on a gridline, and she wants no more than 10 gridlines above 0. What should the scale go up in?
items.e: Counting in 5s needs 10 gridlines (5 to 50), and every number is in the 5 times table. 1s or 2s need far too many lines (50 or 25). In 10s, 35 and 45 would end halfway between lines.

items.q: Raffle tickets sold (frequency table): 4A 45, 4B 70, 4C 30, 4D 55. Which column graph shows the same data?
items.e: C matches every number (the scale goes up in 10s). A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: a column is on the line below (it should be halfway between two lines); D: one column is one line too high.

items.q: Ice blocks sold (frequency table): Mon 20, Tue 30, Wed 15, Thu 25. Which pictograph shows the same data?
items.e: A matches every number (each symbol = 5). B: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has a symbol too many; D: one row is missing a symbol.
D matches every number (each symbol = 10). A: two rows are the wrong way round; B: a half symbol is drawn as a whole symbol; C: one row has a symbol too many.

items.q: The pictograph and the column graph show the same data. How many tickets should the missing 4C column show?
items.e: Read the 4C row of the pictograph. Each circle = 10 tickets. The 4C row has 3 circles and half a circle: 3 × 10 = 30, and half of 10 is 5, so 30 + 5 = 35 tickets. Draw the 4C column up to 35.
Read the Isla row of the pictograph. Each star = 2 books. The Isla row has 4 stars and half a star: 4 × 2 = 8, and half of 2 is 1, so 8 + 1 = 9 books. Draw the Isla column up to 9.

items.q: How many students read 3 books?
items.e: Each dot is one student. Count the dots above 3: there are 5. (3 is the number of books, not the number of students.)

items.q: How many students are shown on the dot plot?
items.e: Each dot is one student, so count every dot: 2 + 4 + 6 + 5 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 23. (7 counts the stacks, and 28 adds the numbers on the line.)

items.q: What is the most common number of books read?
items.e: The tallest stack of dots is above 2 (6 dots). So 2 books is the most common answer. 6 is how many students, not how many books.

items.q: How many students read more than 4 books?
items.e: More than 4 means 5, 6 or 7 books. There are 2 dots above 5, none above 6 and 1 above 7: 2 + 1 = 3. (6 also counts the students who read exactly 4.)

items.q: Which statement is true?
c: The same number of students read 2 books and 3 books.
More students read 1 book than 5 books.
Every student read at least 1 book.
items.e: 1 book has 4 dots and 5 books has 2 dots, so this is true. Only 1 student read 7 books. 2 students read 0 books. 2 books has 6 dots and 3 books has 5.

items.q: How many students have no brothers or sisters?
items.e: No brothers or sisters means the answer 0. There are 4 dots above 0.

items.q: How many students have 2 or more brothers and sisters?
items.e: 2 or more means 2, 3, 4 or 5: 6 + 3 + 0 + 2 = 11. (5 leaves out the students with exactly 2.)

items.q: How many more students have 1 brother or sister than have 3?
items.e: Above 1 there are 9 dots. Above 3 there are 3 dots. 9 − 3 = 6. (2 is 3 − 1, the numbers on the line, not the dots.)

items.q: Grace asked 4A, “How many brothers and sisters do you have?” She wants to show each answer as one dot above a number line. Which display should she use?
items.e: A dot plot has a number line, and each answer is one dot above its number. It suits numerical data such as 0, 1, 2 or 3 brothers and sisters.

items.q: Kai says Graph B shows fewer cans than Graph A because its columns are shorter. Is he right?
c: Yes. The columns in Graph B are shorter.
No. Graph B shows more cans.
Yes. Graph B has fewer gridlines.
No. Both graphs show the same numbers.
items.e: Graph A goes up in 5s and Graph B goes up in 10s. Read both: 4A 20, 4B 35, 4C 40, 4D 25. The numbers are the same; only the scale is different. Always read the scale, not the height.

items.q: Read Graph B. How many cans did 4B collect?
items.e: Graph B goes up in 10s. The 4B column ends halfway between 30 and 40, so it shows 35. (3 counts the grid spaces. Graph A shows 35 too.)

items.q: How many more students chose netball than cricket?
items.e: The scale goes up in 5s. Netball 30, cricket 15. How many more means subtract: 30 − 15 = 15. (3 counts the grid spaces between the tops of the columns.)

items.q: Every Year 4 student voted once. How many students are in Year 4?
items.e: Read every column: 25 + 15 + 30 + 20 + 10 = 100. (20 counts grid spaces: 5 + 3 + 6 + 4 + 2.)

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the graph?
c: Most children in Australia like AFL best.
More Year 4 students chose netball than any other sport.
items.e: Netball has the tallest column (30), so this is supported. The survey asked about favourites, not who plays. 10 students chose swimming. The survey only asked Year 4, not all of Australia.

items.q: Cooper says, “Twice as many students chose AFL as chose swimming.” Is he right?
c: No. Twice 10 is 20, but AFL got 25.
No. AFL got 5 and swimming got 2.
Yes. AFL got 25 and swimming got 10.
Yes. AFL is the most popular sport.
items.e: Swimming 10, AFL 25. Twice 10 is 20, and 25 is more than 20, so he is not right. (5 and 2 are grid spaces, not students.)

items.q: The school will buy new equipment for the two most popular sports. Which two?
items.e: The two tallest columns are netball (30) and AFL (25). Soccer is 20.

items.q: How many students come to school by car?
items.e: Each circle stands for 10 students. The Car row has 8 circles: 8 × 10 = 80. (8 reads each circle as 1 student.)

items.q: How many more students come by car than walk?
items.e: Car: 8 circles = 80. Walk: 4 circles and half a circle = 40 + 5 = 45. 80 − 45 = 35. (Leaving out the half circle gives 80 − 40 = 40.)

items.q: How many students walk, ride a bike or ride a scooter?
items.e: Walk 45, Bike 20, Scooter 15 (1 circle and half a circle). 45 + 20 + 15 = 80. (Leaving out the half circles gives 40 + 20 + 10 = 70. 8 counts the circles.)

items.q: Next term, 20 students who come by car will walk instead. What should the Walk row show then?
items.e: Walk now: 45. 45 + 20 = 65 students. 65 = 60 + 5: 6 circles for 60 and half a circle for 5.

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the pictograph?
c: The bus is the least common way to travel.
No students come to school by train.
More students come by car than walk and ride a scooter together.
items.e: Car 80. Walk and scooter: 45 + 15 = 60. 80 is more, so this is supported. Walking (45) is not most of the 195 students. Train was not in the survey, so we cannot tell. Scooter (15) is the least common.

items.q: How many students read at least 3 books?
items.e: At least 3 means 3, 4 or 5 books: 6 + 3 + 1 = 10 students. (4 leaves out the students who read exactly 3. 21 is the students who read 3 or fewer.)

items.q: How many books did these students read altogether?
items.e: Multiply each number of books by its frequency: 0 × 2 + 1 × 5 + 2 × 8 + 3 × 6 + 4 × 3 + 5 × 1 = 0 + 5 + 16 + 18 + 12 + 5 = 56. (25 is the number of students, and 15 adds 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5.)

items.q: Which conclusion is supported by the table?
c: Every student in 4D read at least one book.
Nobody read 6 books because the books were too long.
Most students in 4D read 2 or 3 books.
4D read more books than every other class.
items.e: 2 or 3 books: 8 + 6 = 14 of the 25 students, which is more than half. 2 students read 0 books. The table has no data about other classes, and it does not tell us why.

items.q: The teacher says, “More than half the class read 2 or more books.” Is she right?
c: No. 7 students read fewer than 2 books.
items.e: 2 or more books: 8 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 18 students. Half of 25 is 12 and a half, and 18 is more, so she is right.

items.q: Zara wants to know which ice block flavour the canteen should sell. Which survey question is best?
c: Which flavour would you choose: lemon, raspberry, mango or cola?
How many ice blocks are in the freezer?
Raspberry is the best flavour, isn’t it?
items.e: The best question matches the purpose and gives clear answers to count. “Do you like ice blocks?” does not tell her the flavour, and the last question pushes people to say raspberry.

items.q: Ethan wants to find out how Year 4 students travel to school. Who should he ask?
c: Only the students on the bus
items.e: To answer a question about Year 4, collect data from Year 4. Asking only friends or only bus students would give answers that do not show the whole of Year 4.

items.q: Mia types the house points into a spreadsheet: Banksia 40, Wattle 65, Waratah 50, Jacaranda 55. Her column graph goes up in 10s. Where is the top of the Wattle column?
items.e: The gridlines go 0, 10, 20 … There is no line for 65. 65 is halfway between 60 and 70.

items.q: Mia also wants a pictograph of the house points (40, 65, 50 and 55). She can use whole and half symbols, and she wants as few symbols as she can. Which key should she use?
items.e: With a key of 10: 4, 6 and a half, 5 and 5 and a half symbols (21 symbols). A key of 5 needs 42 symbols, and a key of 1 or 2 needs even more.

items.q: How many more students chose netball or soccer than chose AFL or cricket?
items.e: Step 1: netball or soccer: 30 + 20 = 50. Step 2: AFL or cricket: 25 + 15 = 40. Step 3: 50 − 40 = 10. (2 counts grid spaces.)

items.q: The school bike racks hold 30 bikes. All the students who ride a bike park there. How many spaces are left?
items.e: The Bike row has 2 circles: 2 × 10 = 20 bikes. 30 − 20 = 10 spaces. (28 reads each circle as 1 bike.)
